Autobiographical memory was impaired across time periods in AD and FTL patients; however, recent autobiographical memory was most vulnerable in FTD at the follow-up assessment, and neuroimaging analyses revealed a time-specific role for discrete cortical regions in autobiographical memory retrieval.

1) autobiographical memory (memory for events from one's personal past) is compromised in both Alzheimer's disease and FTD, 2) this memory impairment is progressive over time, and 3) the brain regions responsible for this memory impairment differ between Alzheimer's disease and the two variants of FTD.
Autobiographical memory was impaired in both Alzheimer's disease (a common form of dementia) and frontotemporial dementia (a rare form of dementia).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of autobiographical memory ( ABM ) impairments in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and frontotemporall lobar degeneration (FTD).
the nature and neural underpinnings of autobiographical memory in healthy ageing and dementia.
the nature of autobiographical memory in dementia and the role of brain networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present study provides evidence that the autobiographical memory impairment in Alzheimer's disease is not progressive, and that the impairment in frontotemporal dementias is progressive.
the findings are in line with our hypothesis that the posterior cingulate and parietal cortices are crucial for autobiographical memory retrieval in the FTD patients.

the authors have shown that the posterior parietal cortex plays a crucial role in the recent autobiographical memory in the context of FTD and the temporal lobe is crucial for the remote autobiographical memory in AD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the progressive spread of degeneration in AD and FTL is associated with a time‐specific loss of memory for events from different life epochs.
the autobiographical memory impairment in dementia is time‐specific and that the posterior parietal regions are crucial for recent autobiographic memory.
autobiographical memory is vulnerable in dementia and that it is vulnerable in different ways depending on the disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are different patterns of autobiographical memory loss in Alzheimer's and FTD.
autobiographical memory is not only vulnerable to disruption early in the course of neurodegenerative diseases, but is also particularly susceptible to decline with advancing disease severity.
the progressive loss of autobiographical memories with advancing dementia is not uniform across life epochs.
